findings.title: Reaction-key drift lock still fails OPEN on access-modifier-prefixed fields — both Node locks (pre-commit hook and the 'derived' emulator payload) go green on the exact drift class a6 exists to catch
findings.trace: The round-14 regex is `/^\s*(?:@\w+(?:\([^)]*\))?\s+)*(?:var|let)\s+(\w+)\s*[:=]/gm` (drift-check.mjs:46). The optional prefix group accepts ONLY @-attributes; a bare Swift access/storage modifier before var|let kills the match because `^\s*` is immediately followed by a required attribute-or-var|let. I ran the exact regex against DropReaction's body plus one added field: baseline -> 5 keys; `private var clientVersion: String = "1"` -> 5 keys; `public var ...` -> 5; `private(set) var ...` -> 5; `lazy var ...` -> 5. (`let schema: Int = 2` -> 6 and `@ServerTimestamp var commitAt: Date?` -> 6, so round 14's stated widenings do work.) The fail-closed guard at drift-check.mjs:49 (`keys.length < 3`) cannot fire because the 5 known fields still parse. Consequence chain: appReactionKeys() returns the stale 5 names, so (1) the pre-commit hook (.githooks/pre-commit:8) reports 'reaction key drift check OK'; and (2) rules.test.mjs:104 iterates those same 5 names, so its `if (!(key in sampleValues)) throw` fail-closed guard at :106 never fires and the suite writes the OLD 5-key payload — meaning the comment at rules.test.mjs:96-98 ('the emulator payload is DERIVED from the app's actual DropReaction fields — if the struct grows a field, this suite writes what the app will write and fails the moment the rules refuse it') is false for this edit class. Only ReactionShapeTests.swift:12 (device suite, JSONEncoder — which does encode private stored properties) still catches it. Two of the three locks fail open, and they are the two that gate the rules deploy from the command line.
findings.harm: A developer adds `private var clientVersion: String` (or any modifier-prefixed field) to DropReaction. `npm test` in web/rules-tests passes and the pre-commit hook passes, both explicitly certifying no reaction-key drift. firestore.rules:78 `keys().hasOnly(['id','emoji','uid','byName','at'])` then rejects every real reaction write. FirestoreAcked maps that permission-denied through DropStoreError.terminalRefusalReason (FirebaseDropStore.swift:246) to refusedByServer — a terminal verdict. Every emoji tap in the app fails permanently, which is precisely the risk the log itself ranks as pre-deploy priority 2 (COUNSEL-WAVE-C-LOG.md:73: 'first post-deploy reaction under a drifted struct = permission-denied -> terminal -> the loop's payoff dies').
findings.fix: Allow non-@ declaration modifiers in the prefix group while still excluding type-level and computed members, e.g. `/^\s*(?:(?:@\w+(?:\([^)]*\))?|private(?:\(set\))?|fileprivate(?:\(set\))?|internal|public|open|final|lazy|weak|unowned(?:\((?:safe|unsafe)\))?|nonisolated)\s+)*(?:var|let)\s+(\w+)\s*[:=](?![^\n]*\{\s*$)/gm`, keeping `static`/`class` unmatched (Codable ignores them) and dropping computed properties via the trailing-brace lookahead. Add a Node self-test that feeds fixture struct bodies through an exported parse(source) helper and asserts each modifier form yields 6 keys — the current regex has no test of its own, so both its round-14 widenings and its fail-closed threshold are unexercised.

findings.title: The loss ledger's 'Clear' control is inert on the skipped-rows path — acknowledgeLosses() is undone by the very next refresh, permanently, because round 14 made Dismiss non-destructive
findings.trace: refresh()'s memory switch re-derives the ledger from the load outcome on EVERY pass: DropStore.swift:679-688 `case .skippedRows(_, _, let lostIDs)?: ... for id in lostIDs { markLost(id) }`. LocalDropStore.loadDrops sets lastOutcome = .skippedRows at :217 BEFORE the digest check at :224 — the .ackdigest suppresses only pendingReadWarning, never the outcome — so a dismissed-but-still-present bad file yields .skippedRows with the same lostIDs forever. Round 14 deliberately stopped Dismiss from rewriting the file (:276-291), so the bad rows persist indefinitely; nothing in the app removes them except a subsequent save() (LocalDropStore.save :347-351 reloads, drops the bad rows, and persists the survivors), which is not something the loss rung prompts. acknowledgeLosses() (:1263-1266) clears lostRowIDs with no durable record of the acknowledgement, so the next markLost re-inserts every id. Refresh triggers are frequent and unavoidable: AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:52 refreshes on every scenePhase .active, plus RootView.swift:168 on launch, DropsListScreen.swift:26 pull-to-refresh, MapScreen.swift:106, and acknowledgeReadIncident's own kicked refresh (DropStore.swift:789). D3 — the test is vacuous with respect to this: testLostRowsAreRecordedDurablyAndDismissDestroysNothing (DropStoreTests.swift:1319-1320) calls acknowledgeLosses() then asserts lostRowIDs.isEmpty and ENDS; it never refreshes afterwards, so it passes identically with and without the defect.
findings.harm: User has drops.json with one unreadable row. The ladder shows '1 drop was lost to a storage problem' with a Clear button (ProfileScreen.swift:148-164). The user taps Clear; the rung disappears. They background the app and return — AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:52 refreshes, markLost re-fires, and the identical rung is back. This repeats forever with no user action that can retire it, which contradicts the exit condition's own contract ('retired ... wholesale by the user (acknowledgeLosses)') and puts a control in the UI whose advertised effect the mechanics cannot back — a charter violation in the same family as the copy findings this wave has been closing.
findings.fix: Give the acknowledgement the same durable shape the .ackdigest gave the banner: persist an `acknowledgedLossIDs` set in acknowledgeLosses() and have markLost skip ids already in it (re-raising only if the id is genuinely destroyed again after a restore, i.e. clear the acknowledgement in clearLost). Then extend DropStoreTests.swift:1319 with an `await library.refresh(near: nil); XCTAssertTrue(library.lostRowIDs.isEmpty)` after the Clear — that assertion fails today.

findings.title: Whole-file quarantine records only pendingSyncIDs, so a link-received drop destroyed by a quarantine leaves no ledger entry and the ladder converges to 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'
findings.trace: DropStore.swift:692-696: `if case .quarantinedWholeFile? = localOutcome { for id in pendingSyncIDs { markLost(id) } }`. Own drops that were pending are named; own drops that were acked come back from the owner-scoped cloud query (FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66), so omitting them is correct. Link-received rows are neither: redeem() persists them to disk (:869), enqueueCloudSync returns early for them (:1028) so they are never in pendingSyncIDs, and they carry the sharer's ownerUid so the owner-scoped query never returns them. They are therefore unrecoverable and unrecorded. The library cannot even name them at that point: on a quarantine local.loadDrops returns [] (LocalDropStore.swift:266), merged is empty, and if the cloud read completes, phase 2 at DropStore.swift:641-644 replaces `drops` with the cloud rows only — so the received rows are already gone from `drops` before the memory switch at :678 runs. Convergence to a false all-clear: after the quarantine the journal raises the banner; the user taps Dismiss (DropsListScreen.swift:66 -> acknowledgeReadIncident -> LocalDropStore.acknowledgeIncident, which for .quarantinedWholeFile skips the digest write and just clears the journal at :289); subsequent loads return .absentFile, which keeps localProvablyClean false only via defaults[hadLocalReadIncident] (:711-722). The moment the user creates one new drop, LocalDropStore.save writes a fresh file, the next load is .clean, :698 sets the incident memory false, :723-725 sets hasCompletedCleanRefresh = true, lostRowIDs is empty — and ProfileScreen.swift:172-176 renders 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'.
findings.harm: A user keeps drops received from friends via magic links. drops.json becomes wholly unreadable (device-level corruption, a partial restore, a truncated file from a crash outside the atomic write). Every received drop is destroyed permanently — they cannot be re-fetched by the library, only by the sender re-sending the link — and the app ends up affirmatively claiming the server has confirmed the user's drops, with no rung, no banner and no ledger entry. This is exactly the charter's 'a loss that leaves no record' hole that round 14's ledger was built to close, left open on the destruction path that destroys the most.
findings.fix: On the .quarantinedWholeFile arm, record the rows the library can still name and the cloud provably cannot restore: capture the published id set BEFORE the phase-2 replace (DropStore.swift:641) and, on quarantine, markLost every captured id that the completed cloud read did not return (a positive per-object check, not a set-difference over a narrowed query — the cloud read's serverConfirmedIDs is already available), unioned with pendingSyncIDs as today. Retirement is already wired: clearLost fires on redeem (:873/:880) and on a late save ack (:1064). Add a test that seeds a received drop (receivedViaLink = true) into a real LocalDropStore file, corrupts the file wholesale, refreshes with a cloud store that returns no rows, and asserts library.lostRowIDs contains the received drop's id.

findings.title: The drift-lock pre-commit hook is activated by an uncommitted, undocumented repo-local git config — a fresh clone silently has no lock while the docs assert the repo carries one
findings.trace: `git config --get core.hooksPath` returns `.githooks` and `git config --list --local` shows core.hookspath=.githooks — this lives in .git/config, which is not part of the repository. .git/hooks/ contains only the stock *.sample files, so without that local setting git runs nothing. .githooks/pre-commit IS tracked (confirmed via git ls-files), but nothing in the tree sets core.hooksPath: grep across COUNSEL-WAVE-C-LOG.md, README.md and DECISIONS.md finds no `git config core.hooksPath` instruction, no bootstrap script, and no CI equivalent. Meanwhile COUNSEL-WAVE-C-LOG.md:76 states 'Process: repo under git (.githooks/pre-commit runs both drift locks)' and DECISIONS.md:1182 states 'the repo is under version control with the drift locks as a pre-commit hook' — both true only of this one working copy.
findings.harm: Any fresh clone (a second machine, a rebuild after a repo move, a collaborator, CI) gets the hook file but not the hook. Commits that drift the emoji list or the reaction key set against firestore.rules land unblocked, and the repo's own record says they cannot. This is the failure mode the round-13 researcher named directly (COUNSEL-WAVE-C-LOG.md:73, item 6: 'a checklist run by memory is not a checklist'): the enforcement is a machine-local setting, not a repo-carried one.
findings.fix: Add a one-line bootstrap the docs point at — `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` — as a tracked `make setup` / `scripts/bootstrap.sh` step, and record it in COUNSEL-WAVE-C-LOG.md's Build/verify block next to the npm gate. Verify by cloning the repo to a temp path, running the bootstrap, and confirming a deliberately drifted commit is rejected.

cleanAreas: Digest-suppression mechanism (the lens's primary target) — verified sound. LocalDropStore.swift:302-305 digests the WHOLE file with SHA-256 (8-byte prefix), so suppressed bytes cannot change without re-raising; :224 compares the freshly-read bytes against the sidecar on every load; :240 removes the .ackdigest on any `.clean` load, so the sidecar cannot outlive the content it acknowledged; the `if case .skippedRows?` guard at :284 correctly excludes quarantine and readFailed from suppression, so a persisting real problem keeps re-journaling. Because LocalDropStore is an actor, acknowledgeIncident's re-read of fileURL (:285) cannot interleave with save/delete, and both interleaving orders I traced (ack-then-save, save-then-ack) self-correct through the `.clean` cleanup. No re-journal loop and no destructive rewrite: acknowledgeIncident writes only the sidecar and clears the journal.

Sidecar interaction — preserveUnreadable (:312-323) is content-digest-named and existence-checked, so repeated loads and relaunches of the same bad bytes accumulate exactly one copy, and the 'original kept on disk' claim at :231 is made only when the write actually succeeded (round-10 lens-6 still holds).

Derived emulator payload fail-closed behavior — rules.test.mjs:104-108 throws on any parsed key with no sample value; the throw occurs during argument evaluation, escaping the check() try/catch into module scope, so the process exits non-zero rather than silently skipping. Fails closed for the field-addition case the regex DOES parse.

Drift-check rules-side parsing is unambiguous — firestore.rules contains exactly one `keys().hasOnly([...])` (:78) and one `data.emoji in [...]` (:77), so the first-match regexes at drift-check.mjs:59/24 cannot mis-target; a second hasOnly added elsewhere would produce a loud mismatch, not a silent pass.

ReactionShapeTests.swift:12 is non-vacuous — it fails on an added field, a CodingKeys rename, or a @DocumentID change. Its JSONEncoder proxy for Firestore.Encoder does not fail open on any divergence I could construct (@DocumentID throws, @ServerTimestamp keeps the key name).

Deployed-suite LIST assertion (deployed-rules.test.mjs:63-64) is non-vacuous — the owner-owned seed doc matches the query and is evaluated before the hijack write mutates its ownerUid; it pins the exact query shape FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66 issues on every refresh. Assertion counts verified by enumeration: 30 v3 + 6 deployed-v2, matching the claim.

cloudProven predicate final form (DropStore.swift:966/974) is correct and complete — the terminal clause is gone, the capture is below the received-drop return, and no code path stamps ownerUid locally without a server ack (all six assignment sites traced).

Repository hygiene — 111 tracked files, zero node_modules; the real Secrets.plist and GoogleService-Info.plist are on disk and confirmed ignored, as are web/.firebase and firestore-debug.log; the only tracked plists are a placeholder sample and a credential-free Config/Info.plist. The hook body itself is correct and fail-closed (set -e; import.meta.url-relative paths make it cwd-robust; a missing node blocks the commit).

ReceiveScreen bounded wait (ReceiveScreen.swift:58-68) is cancellation-safe, cannot fire over an already-resolved state, and self-heals when the uid arrives; the .unknown copy claims no cause and offers a working retry.

Test-double fidelity (rule 6) for the round-14 branches — FlakyLocalStore is an actor with real continuation-based suspension on delete and an on-demand save failure; all three previously-unreachable branches are genuinely entered, and testRefreshDuringRemoveDoesNotAbandonTheDelete is a true discriminating test for the round-12 CRITICAL.

findings.title: The loss ledger's only surface is masked by the "Connecting…" and "Uploading N…" rungs
findings.trace: lostRowIDs has exactly one consumer in the app (grep over AugmentMeReality/**: ProfileScreen.swift:148 only — DropsListScreen's banner block, :37-79, does not render it). The ladder is one exclusive if/else chain: terminal (:81) → unresolved deletes (:91) → localReadWarning (:102) → `account.uid == nil` "Connecting…" (:113) → unpushable pending (:117) → lastSyncError (:132) → `uploadingCount > 0` "Uploading N drops…" (:136) → lostRowIDs (:148). Round 14 moved "Connecting…" below the three problem rungs for exactly this reason but placed the NEW permanent-problem rung below both it and a progress rung, contradicting the ladder's own stated doctrine at :74-76 ("problems outrank progress, progress outranks unknown"). Both maskers are unbounded in time: uploadingCount counts pendingSyncIDs with loadable rows (DropStore.swift:522-524) and stays >0 for the whole offline period; uid stays nil for the whole session if anonymous sign-in fails (AccountService never retries in-session — the same fact that forced the ReceiveScreen bounded wait, ReceiveScreen.swift:52-57).
findings.harm: A drop was destroyed by corruption and recorded in the durable ledger. The user dismisses the read banner (which is now digest-suppressed for those bytes, DropStore.swift:224-226, so it never returns) and then goes offline with one unsynced drop. The ladder shows "Uploading 1 drop…"; the loss record is invisible on every screen for as long as the upload stays pending. Same outcome all session when sign-in stalls ("Connecting…"). The ledger exists precisely because banners are dismissible and journals are unreliable — masked by a spinner rung it delivers nothing exit condition (c) promised.
findings.fix: Move the `!library.lostRowIDs.isEmpty` rung up to the problem block — directly after the unresolved-deletes rung and above `account.uid == nil` — or render it as a persistent row of its own outside the exclusive chain (it is a permanent fact, not a state in the sync ladder). Mirroring it in DropsListScreen's banner stack would also remove the single-surface dependency.

findings.title: Losses whose row id cannot be decoded leave no ledger entry at all, and the file rewrite then erases every other trace
findings.trace: LocalDropStore.loadDrops builds the ledger input as `rows.filter { $0.drop == nil }.compactMap(\.id)` (:216) — a row whose id ALSO fails to decode contributes to `skipped` but not to `lostIDs` (FailableDrop.init, :177-189, sets both drop and id to nil when the keyed container or the UUID decode fails — the id-less row class counsel round 2/C9 explicitly anticipated). refresh() then destructures only the ids (:679-688) and discards the `loaded`/`skipped` counts, so nothing durable records that N rows died. Meanwhile persist() (:360-365) writes back only the DECODED rows, so the first subsequent add()/update()/remove()/redeem() — each of which calls save/delete → loadDrops + persist (:347-358) — silently drops the unreadable row from drops.json. The next load is then `.clean`, which sets incidentMemoryKey to false (:698) and lets the latch be re-earned (:711-725). The journaled incident (:325-327) is the only survivor, and it is cleared by the user's Dismiss (:289).
findings.harm: A schema/type corruption garbles one row's id (or the row is written without one). Launch: banner "1 saved drop couldn't be read (original kept on disk)", lostRowIDs stays EMPTY. The user taps Dismiss, then creates any new drop — that save rewrites drops.json without the bad row. Next refresh: `.clean`, incident memory retired, latch earned, ladder shows "Synced — the server has confirmed your drops". The drop is gone, permanently, with zero record anywhere in the app: exactly the "loss that leaves no record" the ledger was built to close, for the corruption class most likely to be unrecoverable.
findings.fix: Record the loss even when the identity is unknown: carry `skipped` into the ledger as a durable count (e.g. a `lostRowCount` companion to lostRowIDs, incremented by `skipped - lostIDs.count`) and render the rung from `lostRowIDs.count + lostRowCount`. Separately, make persist() non-destructive of unreadable rows (round 14's "rows are never deleted" promise currently holds only for the Dismiss path) by re-appending the preserved sidecar bytes or refusing to rewrite while an unacknowledged skip is outstanding.

findings.title: refresh() consumes lastLoadOutcome from a shared slot that a non-mutator save can overwrite without bumping the refresh generation
findings.trace: `lastOutcome` is a single mutable slot on the store actor (:145), rewritten by EVERY load — including the loads that save()/delete() perform internally (:347, :355). refresh() reads it through a separate await (:567) whose only protection is `refreshGeneration` (:568). Every user-facing mutator bumps refreshGeneration at entry (add :898, update :917, remove :936, redeem :851), so those interleavings abort the refresh safely — but performCloudSync's server-stamped write-back, `try await local.save(stamped)` (:1079), is NOT a library mutator and bumps nothing. It also rewrites drops.json through persist(), dropping the unreadable rows. Two such stamped saves landing inside refresh's read window (the first rewrites the file, the second's internal load sets `.clean`) leave refresh consuming a `.clean` verdict that belongs to a different load than the one that produced `merged`.
findings.harm: During the auth-ready reconcile several first-time uploads ack back-to-back and each writes the stamped ownerUid to disk. If two land while a refresh is between its local load and its outcome read, the refresh records no loss (:679-688 never runs), clears incidentMemoryKey (:698), and earns hasCompletedCleanRefresh (:724) over a load that skipped rows — a false all-clear plus a missing ledger entry, with only the dismissible journal left. Narrow timing window (two actor round-trips), machine-driven rather than user-driven, hence LOW; the consequence is identical to state-14-2.
findings.fix: Make the verdict travel with the read instead of living in a slot: have the diagnostics seam return the outcome for a specific load (e.g. `loadDrops` returns `(rows, LocalLoadOutcome)` or stamps a monotonic loadID that refresh captures at call time and re-checks), so a refresh can only consume the verdict of its own load. Alternatively route the stamp write-back through a path that bumps refreshGeneration.

findings.title: acknowledgeLosses() is silently undone by the next refresh while the unreadable bytes remain on disk
findings.trace: LocalDropStore.loadDrops sets `lastOutcome = .skippedRows(...)` (:217-219) BEFORE the acknowledged-digest check (:224), so an acknowledged incident still reports `.skippedRows` on every load. refresh() re-runs `for id in lostIDs { markLost(id) }` unconditionally on that outcome (:688). Round 14 also removed the round-12 rewrite-on-acknowledge, so nothing in the Dismiss path ever removes the bad bytes — the outcome recurs on every load until some unrelated write rewrites the file (:360-365). Refreshes fire on scene-active (AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:52), the Sent tab's refresh button (DropsListScreen.swift:26) and the map (MapScreen.swift:106). D3: the ledger test asserts `lostRowIDs.isEmpty` immediately after acknowledgeLosses (DropStoreTests.swift:1319-1320) and never refreshes again, so it passes identically whether or not the clear is durable.
findings.harm: The user taps Clear on "1 drop was lost to a storage problem"; the rung disappears and returns on the next foreground, every time, for as long as the user does not create/edit/delete something. A user-facing control that reverts itself teaches the user the surface is broken — and the same recurrence keeps hasCompletedCleanRefresh false (:684), so the ladder can never reach any other state either.
findings.fix: Give the ledger the same digest-scoped suppression the banner got: record the acknowledged content digest alongside acknowledgeLosses and skip re-marking ids that came from already-acknowledged bytes (or have LocalDropStore report an `.skippedRowsAcknowledged` outcome for digest-matched content, keeping the latch revocation but not the re-mark).

findings.title: redeem() retires a durable loss record on in-memory presence, which is not evidence the row is persisted
findings.trace: redeem()'s else-branch — taken when `drops.contains(where: { $0.id == drop.id })` (:863) — calls `clearLost(drop.id)` (:880) and performs NO disk write. After round 12's additive phase-1 publish (:578-582) and the cloud merge (:611-623, uid-scoped so all of the owner's rows return, FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66), `drops` routinely holds rows that are NOT on local disk: a stale published copy that survived a quarantine, or a cloud-sourced row that refresh never writes back locally. Retiring a durable loss record is a positive claim ("this row is no longer lost") earned here from evidence a cache/memory copy satisfies — the pattern binding rules 1 and 3 forbid.
findings.harm: An unacked drop is edited offline, the store file is then quarantined (its id is recorded lost at :695), and the stale server copy returns in the next cloud read so `drops` contains the id. The user opens their own link for that drop: redeem takes the else-branch, clears the loss record, and writes nothing to disk. Because the quarantine leaves an ABSENT file, the `.skippedRows` re-mark that would normally repair the record never happens — the loss record is gone permanently while the destroyed local row is not restored. In the `.skippedRows` variant the wrongful retirement self-heals on the next refresh, so harm is bounded to the quarantine path.
findings.fix: Gate clearLost on durable evidence: in the else-branch, persist the row (or verify it is present in the last local load's decoded rows) before retiring the ledger entry; retire on the ack path only when the row is also known to be on disk.

cleanAreas: Per-row epochs (exit a2): rowGenerations is bumped by exactly the four mutators and by nothing else; refresh() correctly does NOT bump it, so the round-12 abandon-the-delete defect is genuinely closed. remove()'s guard, redeem()'s two guards and the supersede semantics behave correctly under every interleaving I could construct from reachable UI flows.

Tombstone suppression is state-based, not ordering-based (DropStore.swift:580-581 phase 1, :642-643 phase 2), so a cloud read that resurrects a row mid-remove cannot outrace the tombstone regardless of which continuation lands first.

cloudProven predicate (a1): sound in both directions — ownerUid is only ever server-sourced, and the capture is correctly below the received-drop return so viewer copies cannot leak unclearable durable entries.

redeem() end to end (a5): disk-before-memory, generation-guarded on both branches, tombstone/attempt/task teardown before the await, recall above the rethrow. The persist-failure path leaves no ghost and genuinely retries.

authDidBecomeReady (seams-3): firstPassThisSession is instance-scoped and set before the awaits; the latch reset stays uid-change-only so the round-12 'pinned at Checking…' regression is not reintroduced; revalidation cannot violate the pending/tombstone assert because remove() clears terminal before tombstoning; accountDidChange is fully deleted with no residual references.

Latch revocation vs sticky evidence (state-2): the destructive-outcome revocation cannot be re-earned in the same pass — localProvablyClean is false for every destructive outcome, and the `.absentFile` arm still requires both a nil warning and a false incident memory. The read-failure early return now records the memory and revokes before returning (flows-lens-4).

Loss ledger's quarantine input (pendingSyncIDs) is defensible: pending ids are always disk-backed at mark time (add/update persist before enqueuing), and the deliberate under-inclusion of acked rows is covered by the uid-scoped (not geo-scoped) cloud read plus the journaled incident.

Test doubles (exit b): FlakyLocalStore parks inside delete before its failure check and fails save deterministically — production's isolation, suspension point and failure modes all reproduced. None of the five round-14 tests is vacuous with respect to its target bug (the one gap is coverage, not vacuity: the ledger test never refreshes after Clear — see state-14-4).

Drift protection and process: both locks run green from the pre-commit hook (core.hooksPath verified), the reaction-key parser fails closed below 3 fields, the emulator payload derives from the app's own struct, and no secrets are tracked.

The permanent loss of R2 is stated nowhere in the app (DropsListScreen.swift:37-79 never renders lostRowIDs either).
findings.harm: After the user dismisses the read banner — the flow round 14 explicitly made safe to dismiss — a permanently destroyed drop is invisible on every surface for as long as any upload is pending (indefinitely, offline) or sign-in has not landed. The only status line the user is shown is a reassuring progress message. This is the charter's 'a loss that leaves no record' state re-created by rung precedence, one round after it was closed.
findings.fix: Move the `!library.lostRowIDs.isEmpty` branch up into the problem block — directly after the localReadWarning rung at :102 and above the `account.uid == nil` rung at :113 (a storage loss is uid-independent and permanent, so nothing transient may mask it). Mirror the rung in DropsListScreen.banners so the 'No drops yet' empty state can never render loss-free. Extract the ladder into a `DropLibrary.statusRung` enum so the order is unit-testable rather than living inline in the View.

findings.title: 'Clear' on the loss rung does not clear — the next automatic refresh re-arms the ledger from the same unreadable rows
findings.trace: acknowledgeLosses() (:1263-1266) empties lostRowIDs and persists the empty set, but records no acknowledgement. refresh()'s skippedRows arm (:679-688) calls markLost(id) unconditionally for every lostID on EVERY pass, and the unreadable rows are never removed from disk (that is round-14's non-destructive-Dismiss guarantee, LocalDropStore.acknowledgeIncident :283-291 stores only a digest). Refresh is automatic and frequent: AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:52 on every scenePhase .active, RootView.swift:168 at auth-ready, MapScreen.swift:106, DropsListScreen.swift:26. So: tap Clear → the rung disappears → background/foreground the app → the identical rung is back. Contrast the banner beside it, which round 14 gave exactly the missing mechanism (digest-keyed suppression that re-raises only for NEW bad bytes, :224). D3: testLostRowsAreRecordedDurablyAndDismissDestroysNothing (DropStoreTests.swift:1285) passes with this defect present — it asserts lostRowIDs.isEmpty at :1320 and never refreshes again.
findings.harm: The only user control over a permanent, unfixable rung is inert: the loss rung cannot be retired for the life of the install, so the Profile status line is pinned to it. Worse for the charter: once the user has cleared it and it returns anyway, a genuinely NEW loss (different rows, a later incident) is indistinguishable from the re-armed old one — the ledger stops carrying information exactly the way an undismissable banner does. The rung's copy ('N drops were lost to a storage problem') also contradicts the banner's 'original kept on disk' for the same rows, with no guidance about what Clear does or what remains recoverable.
findings.fix: Give the ledger the same acknowledgement mechanism the banner got: persist an `acknowledgedLostRowIDs` set (or the acknowledged content digest) in acknowledgeLosses(), and skip markLost for ids already acknowledged — so a NEW lost id still raises the rung while a cleared one stays cleared. Add the copy the rung is missing ('the unreadable rows are still on this device' + what Clear discards).

findings.title: After the bounded wait, 'Try again' can never succeed while the uid is nil — one sign-in attempt per process, and the copy sends the user to check a connection that is not the cause
findings.trace: ReceiveScreen.swift:58-66: uid nil → sleep 10 s → failure = .unknown. The failed view (:132-156) shows 'This link can't be opened right now' / 'It may still be waiting — check your connection and try again in a moment.' and a 'Try again' CTA that calls load() directly (:147-149), bypassing the uid guard. load() → DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop (:65-74) → getDocument(source: .server); with no signed-in user the deployed rules deny it → catch → .unknown. AccountService.start() is invoked exactly once, from AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:30's root .task, and its failure path (AccountService.swift:36-39) only sets statusText 'retrying on next launch' — nothing re-attempts sign-in on scenePhase .active or on demand. So for the whole process lifetime every Try again reproduces the same screen, even after the network returns. (Auth.auth().currentUser is Keychain-persisted, so this is the never-yet-signed-in install — i.e. the first-launch-from-a-link acquisition path this exit condition exists to protect.)
findings.harm: A recipient opening a magic link on a fresh install with flaky network gets a 10-second unlabelled spinner, then a retry loop that cannot terminate and copy that points them at their connection. The one surface that names the real cause ('Couldn't reach the account service — retrying on next launch', ProfileScreen.swift:188-190) is behind a tab this sheet covers. findings.fix: On the bounded-wait timeout, distinguish the cause: render an account-connection state ('We couldn't set up your account on this device — reopen the app to try again') rather than the generic link-unknown copy, and make Try again re-kick AccountService.start() (make start() idempotent/re-entrant) before re-issuing the fetch. findings.title: 'Connecting…' claims an in-flight attempt after sign-in has terminally given up for the session
findings.trace: ProfileScreen.swift:113-116 renders 'Connecting…' for the whole `account.uid == nil` state. AccountService.swift:31-40 makes one signInAnonymously attempt per process; on failure it sets statusText 'Couldn't reach the account service — retrying on next launch' and stops. Nothing is connecting after that point, yet the rung keeps saying so for the rest of the session. The contradicting truth is rendered two lines below in the same Section (:188-190), so the composite surface shows a progress claim and its own refutation simultaneously. Cross-cutting rule 1 (defaults/fallthroughs resolve to UNKNOWN) is what this rung falls through on: a nil uid is three states (not started, in flight, failed) collapsed into the most optimistic one.
findings.harm: A user whose account never came up reads the sync line as 'still working on it' and waits; the state is terminal until relaunch. Low because the honest statusText line is adjacent and no data claim is made.
findings.fix: Publish a tri-state on AccountService (`.connecting` / `.failed(reason)` / `.ready`) and render the failed case as its own rung ('Not connected — reopen the app to retry'), reserving 'Connecting…' for an actually in-flight attempt.

So every subsequent load of the same bad file still reports `.skippedRows` with the same lostIDs. refresh() then re-runs `for id in lostIDs { markLost(id) }` at :688 unconditionally. acknowledgeLosses() (:1263-1266) only empties the set and rewrites the defaults key; it records no suppression of any kind (contrast acknowledgeIncident at :283-291, which DOES persist a content digest). Refresh is not rare: AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:34 (launch) and :52 (every scenePhase .active), MapScreen.swift:106, DropsListScreen.swift:26, DropStore.swift:789 (after banner dismissal), and authDidBecomeReady (:816).
findings.harm: User with one unreadable row in drops.json: dismisses the banner (digest ack), sees 'N drops were lost to a storage problem' with a Clear button, taps Clear — the rung disappears. They background the app and return (or pull-to-refresh, or switch to Explore): the rung is back, unchanged, forever. The only thing that actually stops it is creating or deleting a drop, which rewrites drops.json without the bad rows — a non-obvious action nothing in the UI suggests. The affordance the round-13 exit condition specified ('retired … wholesale by the user') is a no-op the user can never satisfy, and once it is permanently up the ledger can no longer signal a NEW loss (a second corruption just changes a count on a rung that was already showing).
findings.fix: Give the ledger the same suppression discipline the banner got: persist an acknowledged-losses set (or per-id acknowledged flags) alongside lostRowIDs, and have markLost skip ids already acknowledged; clear the acknowledgement for an id only when its row genuinely comes back (redeem restore / late ack) or when new lostIDs appear that are not in the acknowledged set. Alternatively make acknowledgeLosses store the same content digest LocalDropStore already computes, and gate the :688 re-mark on `digest != acknowledgedLossDigest`. Extend testLostRowsAreRecordedDurablyAndDismissDestroysNothing with a post-acknowledgeLosses refresh assertion.

findings.title: The new loss rung is placed below a PROGRESS rung and below the 'Connecting…' UNKNOWN rung, so the charter's permanent loss record is maskable
findings.trace: The ladder is a single else-if chain: terminal :81 (problem) → unresolved :91 (problem) → localReadWarning :102 (problem) → `account.uid == nil` :113 (unknown, 'Connecting…') → unpushable :117 → lastSyncError :132 → `uploadingCount > 0` :136 (PROGRESS) → `!lostRowIDs.isEmpty` :148 (PROBLEM, new in round 14) → 'Checking sync status…' :165 → 'Synced' :172. The file's own header comment at :72-77 states the discipline: 'problems outrank progress, progress outranks unknown'. lostRowIDs is a purely local, uid-independent storage fact (DropStore.swift:679-696), yet it is gated behind both a progress rung and an unknown rung. This is the same class round 13 raised as the seams-1 tail and round 14 fixed for the other three rungs 35 lines above.
findings.harm: Two reachable maskings. (1) Progress: user has a recorded loss and one drop pending upload while offline — uploadingCount stays > 0 for the whole offline period (DropStore.swift:522-524 counts pendingSyncIDs ∩ drops), so 'Uploading 1 drop…' hides 'N drops were lost to a storage problem' indefinitely. (2) Unknown: AccountService.start() (AccountService.swift:31-40) never retries anonymous sign-in within a session, so an offline cold launch leaves account.uid nil for the entire session; if the corruption banner was dismissed on an earlier run (localReadWarning nil), the ladder shows 'Connecting…' and the loss record is invisible until the next successful sign-in. In both cases the app's only surface for permanently destroyed drops is hidden — lostRowIDs is rendered nowhere else (grep: ProfileScreen.swift:148/156/162 are its only view references; DropsListScreen's banner stack at :39-69 has no loss rung).
findings.fix: Move the `!library.lostRowIDs.isEmpty` branch up into the problem block — directly after the localReadWarning rung at :102 and above the `account.uid == nil` rung at :113. Consider also surfacing it in DropsListScreen.banners (the tab where drops are actually managed), since that is where a user notices rows are missing.

findings.title: A superseded remove() leaves a memory-only row: the disk row is already destroyed, no tombstone is written, no cloud delete is issued — and the round-14 test asserts this state as correct
findings.trace: remove() destroys the disk row at :942 (`try await local.delete(drop)`), then at :952 aborts the entire remainder if another mutator bumped the row epoch. redeem()'s row-exists branch (:879-881) does NO disk write — it assumes an in-memory row implies a disk row. update(_:persist:false) (:916-924) likewise inserts/updates `drops` with no persist. So the interleaving remove→(epoch bump by redeem or a non-persisting update)→remove-resume ends with the id present in `drops`, absent from local storage, with no pendingDeleteIDs entry and no launchCloudDelete. testRedeemDuringRemoveSupersedesTheDelete (DropStoreTests.swift:1196-1217) drives exactly this sequence and asserts only `library.drops.contains{...}` at :1216 — it never asserts the disk row, so it would pass identically whether or not redeem re-persists.
findings.harm: For a link-received drop (the case the test itself uses, receivedViaLink = true at :1207) the cloud refresh is owner-scoped (FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66), so nothing restores it: the drop is visible in the library for the rest of the session and then silently vanishes at the next refresh's phase-2 replace (DropStore.swift:641-645) or on relaunch. That is a silent loss of a redeemed drop — the exact class exit condition a5 was written to close on the other branch. Reachability is genuinely narrow: it needs a redeem (or a non-persisting AR live-edit Task) for the SAME id to land inside the single local-file-write window of remove(), i.e. a same-instant cross-surface double action by one user; I could not construct a sequential UI path that reaches it. Reported at LOW on that basis, not dismissed, because the test currently locks in the wrong invariant.
findings.fix: In redeem()'s row-exists branch (:879-881), persist the row (or re-persist the merged row) rather than assuming disk parity — the same disk-first discipline :863-878 already uses. Additionally, in remove()'s abort branch at :952-955, re-assert disk state for the surviving row instead of returning silently. Strengthen testRedeemDuringRemoveSupersedesTheDelete to assert the row is on disk after releaseAllDeletes (read back through the local store), which is what makes the assertion meaningful.

LocalDropStore.loadDrops sets `lastOutcome = .skippedRows(loaded:skipped:lostIDs:)` at DropStore.swift:217-219 BEFORE the acknowledged-digest check at :224, and the digest only nils `pendingReadWarning` — it never changes the machine-checkable outcome. Round 14 also stopped Dismiss rewriting the file, so the bad rows persist indefinitely; the only thing that removes them is an unrelated save (LocalDropStore.save :344-351 reloads, drops undecodable rows, persists survivors), which nothing in the UI prompts. Charter class: a user control whose advertised effect the mechanics cannot back, same family as the copy defects this wave spent six rounds closing. verdicts.industrialSolution: Give the ledger the same acknowledgement discipline the banner got in this very round — the fix is already designed, just not applied to the second surface. Persist `acknowledgedLostRowIDs` (a second defaults set alongside lostRowIDs) in acknowledgeLosses(); have markLost skip ids present in it; have clearLost remove the id from BOTH sets so a genuine restore re-arms the ability to record a future loss of the same id. That keeps the two properties that matter: a cleared loss stays cleared, and a NEW lost id still raises the rung. The alternative shape — have LocalDropStore report a distinct `.skippedRowsAcknowledged` outcome for digest-matched content — is worse here, because the latch revocation at :684 SHOULD keep firing (the file genuinely still has unreadable rows), and splitting the outcome invites someone to skip the revocation too. verdicts.industrialSolution: Two changes. verdicts.reasoning: Traced end to end and it holds. ReceiveScreen.swift:57-68: uid nil → 10 s sleep → `failure = .unknown`. The failed view (:132-156) renders 'This link can't be opened right now' / 'It may still be waiting — check your connection and try again in a moment.' with a Try again CTA at :146-149 that calls `load()` directly, bypassing the uid guard entirely. load() (:163-172) → DropSharingService.fetchSharedDrop (:65-105) → `getDocument(source: .server)`; firestore.rules:52-54 requires `signedIn()` for get, so with no current user the read is permission-denied → the catch at :72-74 returns .unknown → the same screen. So for the whole process lifetime, every Try again reproduces the same screen even after the network returns. Because Auth.auth().currentUser is Keychain-persisted, this is specifically the never-yet-signed-in install — i.e. first-launch-from-a-link, the exact acquisition path exit condition (a3) exists to protect. Charter class: a retry affordance and a causal instruction ('check your connection') that the mechanics cannot back. NOT an exit-condition failure — round 14 built precisely what round 13 specified (bounded wait → honest .unknown + Try again) — this is a new finding about the honesty of the state it now reliably reaches. Severity MEDIUM on the acquisition path.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Make the retry re-attempt the thing that is actually broken. Two parts, both small. (1) Make AccountService.start() idempotent and re-entrant — guard on an `isSigningIn` flag rather than on call-site discipline — and call it from the scenePhase .active handler alongside the library refresh; that alone converts 'terminal until force-quit' into 'self-heals on the next foreground', which is the standard iOS anonymous-auth pattern (Firebase's own guidance is to re-attempt on app-foreground, since the SDK does not retry a failed signInAnonymously). (2) Distinguish the cause at the bounded-wait timeout: when uid is nil, render an account-connection state ('We couldn't set up your account on this device') and wire Try again to `await account.start()` before re-issuing the fetch. Surfacing account.statusText inside ReceiveScreen when uid is nil is a cheap partial that at least stops the copy blaming the network — today the one line that names the real cause (ProfileScreen.swift:187-189) is behind a tab this sheet covers.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified against the decoder. FailableDrop (DropStore.swift:170-189) sets BOTH `drop` and `id` to nil when the keyed container or the UUID decode fails, and loadDrops builds the ledger input as `rows.filter { $0.drop == nil }.compactMap(\.id)` at :216 — so a row whose id ALSO fails to decode raises `dropped` but contributes nothing to lostIDs. refresh() destructures only the ids at :679-688 and discards the loaded/skipped counts. Then the erasure completes: LocalDropStore.persist (:360-365) writes back only the DECODED rows, so the first subsequent add/update/remove/redeem — each of which routes through save/delete → loadDrops + persist (:344-358) — silently drops the unreadable row from drops.json. The next load is `.clean`, which at :698 sets incidentMemoryKey false; localProvablyClean (:711-722) then returns true, hasCompletedCleanRefresh is re-earned at :724, lostRowIDs is empty, and ProfileScreen.swift:172-176 renders 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops'. The journaled incident (:325-327) is the only survivor and the user's Dismiss clears it (:289). That is a complete, traced path from a destroyed drop to an affirmative all-clear with zero record in the app — the exact charter hole the ledger was built to close, left open for the corruption class where the identity itself is garbled (a byte flip in the id field, a row written as a non-object, a future schema change to the id type). Note this class is NOT covered by the round-10 own-1 discipline the code comment at :247-250 claims, because that discipline governs the journal, not the machine-checkable memory. Severity MEDIUM: real silent loss, but requires the id specifically to be undecodable.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Two independent hardenings; do the first, consider the second. (1) Record the loss even when the identity is unknown: add a durable `lostRowCount` companion to lostRowIDs, incremented by `skipped - lostIDs.count` in the skippedRows arm, and render the rung from `lostRowIDs.count + lostRowCount`. This is the minimum that satisfies the charter — 'we destroyed N rows and cannot name them' is an honest record; 'Synced' is not. It also closes F-SEAMS-14-3 with the same mechanism (see that verdict). (2) The stronger, more industrial fix is to stop persist() from silently completing the destruction: a store that rewrites a file it could not fully parse is a lossy round-trip, which is why production Codable pipelines either preserve unknown/undecodable payload verbatim (keep the raw JSONValue for failed rows and re-emit them on write) or refuse to rewrite while an unacknowledged skip is outstanding. The first option makes round 14's 'rows are never deleted' promise true for ALL paths rather than only for Dismiss, and it makes the loss recoverable rather than merely recorded. Test: seed `[good, {"heightAboveGround":"3"}]` (no id at all), refresh, assert a durable record exists; add() a drop; refresh; assert the record still stands and hasCompletedCleanRefresh was not silently re-earned.

verdicts.reasoning: Mechanically exact. DropStore.swift:692-696 marks only `pendingSyncIDs` on the quarantine arm. I verified link-received rows are in neither escape hatch: redeem() persists them to disk (:869) but enqueueCloudSync returns early for them (:1027 `guard drop.receivedViaLink != true else { return }`), so they are never pending; and I grepped every local-store write in the file (lines 544, 869, 901, 926, 942, 1079) to confirm refresh NEVER writes cloud rows back to disk — combined with the owner-scoped cloud query (FirebaseDropStore.swift:64-66), a received row destroyed by a quarantine is unrecoverable by the library. The convergence to a false all-clear is real and I walked it: quarantine → loadDrops returns [] (:266) → incidentMemory true, latch revoked (:690-691), journal raises the banner → user taps Dismiss (for .quarantinedWholeFile the `if case .skippedRows?` guard at :284 skips the digest write and just clears the journal at :289) → subsequent loads return .absentFile, which cannot earn the latch because localProvablyClean requires `!defaults.bool(forKey: incidentMemoryKey)` (:715-719) → the user creates ONE new drop → save writes a fresh file → next load is .clean → :698 sets incidentMemory false → :724 earns the latch → 'Synced — the server has confirmed your drops', with the received drops permanently gone and no rung, no banner, no ledger entry. One correction to the finding's fix, which I checked and it does not fully work: capturing the published id set before the phase-2 replace (:641) only helps if those rows were published in THIS session — on a cold launch into a corrupt file, `drops` is empty and nothing can name them. Severity MEDIUM. Note this is not an exit-condition failure: round 13 specified the quarantine arm record pendingSyncIDs and round 14 built exactly that; the gap is in the spec, which is what a final audit is for.
verdicts.industrialSolution: The same `lostRowCount` mechanism state-14-2 needs also closes this, and closes the cold-launch case the id-capture fix cannot. On the .quarantinedWholeFile arm: union pendingSyncIDs into lostRowIDs as today, AND set a durable un-nameable-loss flag whose retirement requires explicit user acknowledgement — never a later `.clean` load. That is the round-10 own-1 discipline ('a clean load says nothing about the rows already destroyed') applied to the machine-checkable memory, which currently violates it at :698 by auto-retiring incidentMemoryKey on `.clean`. Concretely: split the durable memory into `hadLocalReadIncident` (auto-retired by .clean — fine, it gates the latch) and `unacknowledgedDestruction` (retired only by acknowledgeLosses), and gate the 'Synced' rung on the latter. Additionally, do capture the published id set before the phase-2 replace and markLost every captured id the completed cloud read did not return — that is a positive per-object check against serverConfirmedIDs, not a set-difference over a narrowed query (binding rule 2), and it upgrades the warm-session case from 'N unnamed' to named ids that clearLost can retire via redeem (:873/:880) or a late ack (:1064). Test: seed a receivedViaLink row plus an acked own row into a real LocalDropStore file, corrupt the file wholesale, refresh against a cloud store returning only the own drop, assert a durable loss record exists and that a subsequent clean load cannot reach 'Synced'.

verdicts.reasoning: Verified directly. `git config --get core.hooksPath` returns `.githooks`; `ls .git/hooks` shows only the stock *.sample files, so without that setting git runs nothing on commit. .githooks/pre-commit IS tracked (git ls-files confirms it is the only tracked hook/script file — there is no Makefile, no scripts/ directory) and its body is correct and fail-closed (`set -e`; `node web/rules-tests/drift-check.mjs`, which resolves its Swift and rules paths from import.meta.url so it is cwd-robust; a missing node aborts the commit). verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed empirically, not by inspection: I extracted the exact regex from drift-check.mjs:44-48 into a standalone harness and ran nine fixtures. `private var clientVersion: String = "1"` → 5 keys; `public var` → 5; `private(set) var` → 5; `lazy var` → 5. The optional prefix group accepts ONLY @-attributes, and `^\s*` is immediately followed by a required attribute-or-var|let, so any bare declaration modifier kills the match. The fail-closed guard at :49 (`keys.length < 3`) cannot fire because the five known plain-`var` fields still parse. The consequence chain is real: appReactionKeys() returns the stale 5 names, so the pre-commit hook reports OK, and rules.test.mjs:104's `if (!(key in sampleValues)) throw` fail-closed guard never fires because it iterates the same stale 5 — so the suite writes the OLD payload and the comment claiming the payload is derived from the app's actual fields is false for this edit class. Swift's synthesized Codable encodes stored properties regardless of access level, so a `private var` DOES reach the wire and firestore.rules:78 `hasOnly(['id','emoji','uid','byName','at'])` would reject every reaction write. I DOWNGRADE severity from MEDIUM to LOW on one verified ground the finding acknowledges but underweights: ReactionShapeTests.swift:12 encodes with JSONEncoder, which also encodes private stored properties, and asserts the exact 5-key set — so the drift IS caught, by the device suite, which COUNSEL-WAVE-C-LOG.md:87 and the round-14 process note both document as required before any rules deploy. The harm chain therefore requires skipping the documented gate. Two useful confirmations for the record: round 14's stated widenings genuinely work (`let schema: Int = 2` → 6; `@ServerTimestamp var commitAt: Date?` → 6, which is exactly the residual a6 was aimed at), and the computed-property false positive (`var summary: String { emoji }` → 6) fails in the safe direction.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Widen the prefix group to non-@ declaration modifiers and exclude computed members, keeping static/class unmatched since Codable ignores type-level members: `/^\s*(?:(?:@\w+(?:\([^)]*\))?|private(?:\(set\))?|fileprivate(?:\(set\))?|internal|public|open|final|lazy|weak|unowned(?:\((?:safe|unsafe)\))?|nonisolated)\s+)*(?:var|let)\s+(\w+)\s*[:=](?![^\n]*\{\s*$)/gm`. But the regex is the symptom; the structural point is that this parser has NO test of its own — neither of round 14's two widenings nor its fail-closed threshold is exercised anywhere, which is why the third widening it needed was never noticed. Export a pure `parseReactionKeys(source)` from drift-check.mjs and add a Node self-test asserting 6 keys for each modifier form, 5 for `static let`, and 5 for a computed property, plus a fixture that trips the <3 threshold. A lock without a test of the lock is the same class of defect this wave has been closing in the app. Longer term, the genuinely robust version of this check is to stop regexing Swift and derive the key list from the encoder output the app already produces — i.e. make ReactionShapeTests write its encoded key set to a checked-in fixture that the Node suite reads — which collapses three locks with three failure modes into one source of truth.

verdicts.reasoning: Holds on the facts, and I confirmed the missing retry myself. ProfileScreen.swift:113-115 renders 'Connecting…' for the entire `account.uid == nil` state, which collapses three distinct conditions — not started, in flight, and terminally failed — into the most optimistic one. AccountService.swift:27-40 makes exactly one signInAnonymously attempt per process; on failure it sets statusText 'Couldn't reach the account service — retrying on next launch' and stops, and AugmentMeRealityApp.swift:35-54's scenePhase .active handler never re-invokes start(). So nothing is connecting, and the rung keeps claiming it for the rest of the session. This is a binding-rule-1 violation in the literal sense: a fallthrough resolving to the good/progress state rather than to UNKNOWN. Severity LOW, and I hold it there for a reason the finding states honestly: the contradicting truth is rendered in the SAME Section two lines below (ProfileScreen.swift:187-189 renders account.statusText in orange), so the composite surface shows both the optimistic claim and its refutation, and no data claim is made. The harm is a user who reads the sync line and waits for something that will never happen — real, but bounded and self-disclosed.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Publish a tri-state on AccountService rather than inferring connection state from a nil uid: `enum Connection { case idle, connecting, failed(String), ready }`, set to .connecting before the signInAnonymously await and to .failed in the catch. Render .failed as its own rung ('Not connected — reopen the app to retry') and reserve 'Connecting…' for an actually in-flight attempt. This is the same fix SURF-14-3 needs on the receive side, and doing both from one tri-state is the reason to do it: the two findings are one missing state machine observed from two screens. If start() is also made re-entrant and called on foreground (see SURF-14-3), the .failed rung becomes self-healing and the copy can honestly say 'Reconnecting…' on the next foreground.

verdicts.reasoning: The mechanism is real and I verified every link. `lastOutcome` is a single mutable slot on the LocalDropStore actor (DropStore.swift:145), rewritten by EVERY load, including the loads that save() and delete() perform internally (:344, :355). refresh() reads it through a separate await at :567-569 whose only protection is `refreshGeneration`. I enumerated all six local-store write sites (lines 544, 869, 901, 926, 942, 1079) and confirmed the finding's key claim: five are user-facing mutators that bump refreshGeneration at entry (add :898, update :917, remove :936, redeem :851) and so abort a racing refresh safely — but performCloudSync's server-stamped write-back at :1079 (`try await local.save(stamped)`) is NOT a library mutator and bumps nothing. It also rewrites drops.json through persist(), which drops the unreadable rows. Two such stamped saves landing inside refresh's read window leave refresh consuming a `.clean` verdict belonging to a different load than the one that produced `merged`, so :679-688 never runs (no loss recorded), :698 clears incidentMemoryKey, and :724 earns hasCompletedCleanRefresh — a false all-clear over a load that skipped rows. Reachable in principle: refresh is @MainActor and awaits the actor three separate times, and the auth-ready reconcile can flush several first-time uploads back-to-back. LOW is the right severity — the window is two actor round-trips, it is machine-driven rather than user-driven, and it requires a simultaneously-unreadable file. The consequence is identical to state-14-2, which is the finding that carries the weight.
verdicts.industrialSolution: Make the verdict travel with the read instead of living in a slot — this is the standard fix for out-of-band diagnostics on a shared actor, and it is small. Change the seam so `loadDrops` returns `(rows, LocalLoadOutcome)` (or stamps a monotonic loadID the caller captures at call time and re-checks when reading the outcome), so a refresh can only ever consume the verdict of its own load. That also lets you delete the separate `lastLoadOutcome()` await entirely, removing one suspension point from refresh's critical section. The cheap interim — routing the stamp write-back through a path that bumps refreshGeneration — works but is worse: it makes a best-effort cache write able to abort a whole refresh pass, trading a rare false all-clear for frequent refresh cancellation. Test with a local-store double whose lastLoadOutcome slot is rewritten by save() (production's shape, per binding rule 6): gate a refresh inside its local read, land two ownerUid-stamp saves, release, and assert the refresh recorded the loss from ITS OWN load.

verdicts.findingId: F3 (flows) / state-14-5 (state) — redeem's row-exists branch assumes memory implies disk
verdicts.reasoning: The mechanism is confirmed; the harm is thinner than either finding claims, and the two reviewers disagree about which consequence matters. Confirmed: redeem()'s else-branch (DropStore.swift:879-881) performs NO disk write — it calls clearLost and returns — and update(persist:false) (:916-924) likewise mutates `drops` without persisting. remove() destroys the disk row at :942 before its post-await epoch guard at :952. So the interleaving remove → (same-row epoch bump by redeem or a non-persisting update) → remove-resume ends with the id in `drops`, absent from disk, no tombstone, no cloud delete. And testRedeemDuringRemoveSupersedesTheDelete (DropStoreTests.swift:1196-1217) does drive exactly that sequence and asserts only `library.drops.contains` at :1216 — it never checks disk, so it would pass whether or not redeem re-persists. That test-invariant criticism is correct and is the durable half of this finding. Where I part company: all three reviewers who looked at this independently reported they could not construct a user-reachable interleaving (redeem's callers are the receive flow; update's are the share sheet and the AR editor; the Sent-tab delete is not co-present with either), and neither can I — it needs a same-instant cross-surface double action on one id inside a single local-file-write window. On state-14-5's variant (clearLost retiring a loss record on memory presence, violating rules 1 and 3), the rule-purity point is valid but the concrete harm is weak: in the quarantine scenario the row IS present in `drops`, IS held by the server, and IS re-published by every refresh — so 'the drop is no longer lost' is a true statement arrived at by a sloppy route, and what was actually lost (an offline edit's newer version) is something the id-keyed ledger never tracked. PARTIAL: mechanism CONFIRMED, test-vacuity CONFIRMED, claimed user-visible harm NOT demonstrated. LOW.
verdicts.industrialSolution: One line of code and one line of test, worth doing because it removes a latent invariant violation cheaply rather than because a user can hit it today. In redeem()'s row-exists branch, persist the row before clearing the ledger entry — `try await local.save(drop)` under the same epoch guard the insert branch uses at :870 — so both branches maintain the same disk/memory parity invariant and the loss retirement rests on a durable write rather than on cache/memory presence (binding rules 1 and 3). Then strengthen testRedeemDuringRemoveSupersedesTheDelete to read the row back through the local store after releaseAllDeletes, so the test locks the invariant that matters instead of the in-memory half. Separately, note for the record that redeem()'s row-exists branch is reachable in a second way nobody filed: because refresh never writes cloud rows to local disk, any cloud-sourced row in `drops` takes this branch, so 'memory implies disk' is false on the normal path too, not just under the racing interleaving — which is the real argument for the fix.
